title: Desmond Tutu and the Truth Commission
text:
When apartheid ended and Nelson Mandela became president in 1994, South Africa faced a hard question: what to do about decades of torture, killings and disappearances. Full trials could take forever and might tear the fragile country apart. A blanket amnesty would deny victims justice. Parliament chose a third way and created the Truth and Reconciliation Commission in 1995, with Archbishop Desmond Tutu as chairman.

From 1996 the commission held public hearings across the country, broadcast on radio and television. Thousands of victims and their families came forward to tell what had happened to them, often for the first time in public. At one early hearing Tutu himself put his head on the table and wept.

Perpetrators could apply for amnesty for politically motivated crimes, but only if they made full disclosure of what they had done. Police officers described in detail how they had tortured and killed activists, sometimes facing the families of their victims.

In October 1998 Tutu presented the commission's final report to Mandela. Tutu argued that there could be no future without forgiveness, but that forgiveness required the truth to be told first.
lesson: Reconciliation needs the truth to be told and heard before forgiveness can be real. Acknowledging what happened is the first step toward healing any broken relationship.
source: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of South Africa Report (1998); Desmond Tutu, No Future Without Forgiveness (1999)
caveat: The commission has been criticized because few perpetrators who were refused amnesty or did not apply were later prosecuted, and reparations to victims were limited.
